title: Mathematicians have drawn a 240-year-old voting paradox as a Klein bottle
body: On 26 October 2026 Quanta Magazine reported work by Ori Livson and Mikhail Prokopenko of the University of Sydney and Siddharth Pritam of the Chennai Mathematical Institute ([Quanta](https://www.quantamagazine.org/how-voting-is-like-a-klein-bottle-20261026/)). It starts from Condorcet’s paradox of 1785: if three equal groups rank Alice > Bob > Carol, Bob > Carol > Alice and Carol > Alice > Bob, then Alice beats Bob, Bob beats Carol and Carol beats Alice, each by two groups to one, so majority voting goes round in a **circle** although every voter is consistent. In 1993 Yuliy Baryshnikov drew each of the six possible rankings as a triangle whose corners are the head-to-head results it implies. Rankings that agree on two results share an edge, and the six close into a tube whose two rims are exactly the circular orders. The new work glues those rims together: glued straight they make a doughnut whose labels don’t match, but glued with a twist they match, and the surface becomes a Klein bottle, which has one side and no edge ([preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07283)).

slides.prompt: Group 1 ranks Alice > Bob > Carol, group 2 Bob > Carol > Alice, group 3 Carol > Alice > Bob. Who wins every head-to-head?
slides.answer: Nobody: each candidate loses one race
slides.detail: Alice beats Bob, Bob beats Carol and Carol beats Alice, each by two groups to one. This is Condorcet’s paradox, from 1785.

slides.alt: Animation on cream paper. Three ballots rank Alice, Bob and Carol; head-to-head counts make a circle of arrows. One ranking becomes a triangle of comparisons; six triangles form a strip that closes into a tube with two coloured rims. Then a wireframe torus, and a Klein bottle.

slides.prompt: Set how many voters are in each of the three groups. Find sizes where majority voting goes round in a circle, with no winner.
slides.takeaway: A circle appears exactly when no group outnumbers the other two together, the rule for the sides of a triangle. Then every candidate loses one head-to-head, and majority rule picks no winner.

slides.heading: Six rankings, six triangles
slides.text: There are 6 ways to rank three candidates. In 1993 mathematician Yuliy Baryshnikov drew each as a triangle whose corners are the head-to-head results it implies, like Alice over Bob. Rankings one swap apart share two results, so their triangles share an edge; the six close into a tube. Its rims are the circular orders.

left.label: Straight
left.text: The tube closes into a doughnut, a torus, but rankings end up glued to the wrong partners.

right.label: With a twist
right.text: Every label matches, and the surface becomes a Klein bottle: one side and no edge.

slides.question: With three groups ranked as in Condorcet’s example, when do majorities go round in a circle?
options: When no group outnumbers the other two
Only when the groups are equal
slides.explanation: Alice beats Bob if groups 1 and 3 outnumber group 2, and so on. All three races go round in a circle exactly when no group is bigger than the other two together.

source.label: Quanta Magazine: How Voting Is Like a Klein Bottle (26 October 2026)
